stops.title: Ping once, then say how sure
stops.silver: You know the feeling of a Sombra on the enemy team. She is there, somewhere, and your screen shows nothing. The page has just split the world in two: what is really there, and what you get shown. When those differ, you still have to act.
stops.do: Sombra hides in one of two rooms, and you cannot see her. Press F to ping. The game then asks how sure you should be that she is where the ping says: left click, right click or melee.
stops.predict: Before you answer, decide what one reading from a ping that is right 8 times in 10 is worth, when you knew nothing a moment ago.
stops.saw: You pressed F, a room lit up, and the honest answer was 80%. You knew nothing before, so the ping's own track record is all you have. Where she really is, nobody shows you. Silver calls that the hidden state, and the ping an observation. This game is a partially observable problem.
stops.agent: A customer's first message names a wish. It is evidence about what they want, not the want itself.

stops.title: Ping again, then pick a room
stops.silver: Two teammates call the same flank and you believe it more than one. One says left, one says right, and you are back to shrugging. The page has just turned that instinct into one number and one rule for moving it.
stops.do: Press F for a second ping and answer how sure you are now. The rooms then open: press F to ping more, or walk onto the pad of the room you think is empty (+10; hers costs 30).
stops.predict: Decide where the bar will land if the second ping agrees with the first, and where it lands if it disagrees.
stops.saw: Two pings that agree put the bar near 94%. One each way sends it straight back to 50%, as if you had never pinged. The purple bar is your belief, and it moved by one rule: keep each room in proportion to how well it explains what you heard. That rule is Bayes' rule. (The coach line after the reveal prices your choice: walking in at your belief, against one more ping.)
stops.agent: Each tool result an agent reads should move its picture of the task the same way, up or down, and by how much it explains.

stops.title: At 80%, walk in or ask again
stops.silver: Holding an ult for the perfect fight costs you fights. Using it on a guess sometimes wastes it. The page has just shown the support version: a question or a lookup only finds things out, but a change to the booking cannot be undone.
stops.do: Round 2: she has moved. Press F once. The question asks whether to walk into the other room now or ping again: left click or right click. Then play the round your way.
stops.predict: Commit to a choice at 80% before you see the arithmetic: is 80% sure enough when the empty room pays 10 and hers costs 30?
stops.saw: 80% feels like a sure thing. Here it is worth 2 on average: 8 times you get 10, twice you lose 30. Pinging on is worth 5.71. One wrong room costs as much as three right ones. So acting on a belief that is not settled is a bet with a price, and the price decides how sure is sure enough.
stops.agent: An agent that cancels a booking at 80% sure has walked into Sombra's room.

stops.title: Same last ping, different bar
stops.silver: Ask someone who walked in mid-fight what happened, and they will tell you about the last kill feed line. It is not enough. The page has just shown a model handed only the latest message, asking the same question in circles, because its last answer was gone.
stops.do: The game asks about two players whose latest ping both said LEFT, with different pings before it: same bar or different bars, left click or right click. Then round 3: ping with F or walk onto a pad, your call.
stops.predict: Decide whether the latest reading alone tells you where the bar is.
stops.saw: Same last ping, different bars: 50% for one player, 94% for the other. The latest reading forgets what came before, and the bar does not. The last ping is not a state. Two situations that look alike are not alike, like the blind runner's square in lesson 11, or the look-alike squares of lecture 7 (where the same view needed different moves).
stops.agent: Before you blame the model, check what it was actually shown on the turn it went wrong.

stops.title: Where a ping is worth most
stops.silver: Checking the scoreboard mid-fight is worth it only if what you see could change your next move. The page has just priced finding out: a lookup is worth a step only when some answer could change what you do.
stops.do: The game asks when one more ping is worth most: at 50% (left click), at 94% (right click), or the same (melee). Then round 4: ping with F or walk onto a pad.
stops.predict: Pick the belief at which a ping is most likely to change which room you walk into.
stops.saw: At 50% a ping beats walking in by about 14.7. At 94% it loses about 0.13. Same ping, same cost. What changed is whether the answer could change your room. Lecture 9 called this the value of information. The plan on the right is value iteration over beliefs (the arithmetic that weighs every future ping): ping between 6% and 94%, walk in outside it.
stops.agent: Looking up a booking to add a bag, which every ticket allows, is a ping at 94%: a turn spent, nothing changed.

stops.title: One ping that is never wrong
stops.silver: Widowmaker's infra-sight does not hint. It shows you. Back in its belief section, the page noted the same thing: a sensor that is always right turns the belief into a fact with one reading.
stops.do: The game asks how many pings you need when the ping is always right: one, two, or three or more. Then round 5, with a ping like Widowmaker's infra-sight: press F, or walk onto a pad.
stops.predict: Decide how far a single perfect reading moves the bar.
stops.saw: One ping, and the bar jumped to 100% or 0%. No more doubt to spend pings on. That is the island's single bump from the hidden wall: one touch and the wall is known. The best plan is worth 9 a round with this ping and 4.71 with the 80% one. In words: a better sensor is worth about 4.3 a round, before you have done anything clever.
stops.agent: Reading the booking itself is a perfect ping. The customer's memory of it is the 80% one.

stops.title: Read what you just did
stops.silver: The page ends where agents actually break: the program wrapped around a model, the harness, picks what the model sees each turn. So it picks the agent's state.
stops.do: Press F to see the debrief. Three lines appear on the left, with your final score and your prediction score.
stops.predict: Before you press, say in one sentence what the purple bar was standing in for.
stops.saw: You pinged to find out, then walked into rooms you could not see into. That is the whole lesson in two moves. The name is partial observability. The bar was a belief state, and a ping was an action you took only for what it told you. (The game is kind to you: two rooms, a known accuracy, and a Sombra who never moves.)
stops.agent: A question or a lookup is a ping, and a cancellation is a room. Check what the agent was shown before you blame it.
